statement: In people dependent on heroin or methadone in supervised withdrawal (12 randomized trials of clonidine, lofexidine or guanfacine against a reducing course of methadone, in a Cochrane review searched to November 2015), the clonidine-type medicines compared with methadone were associated with similar overall withdrawal severity (standardized difference 0.13, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.49; 3 trials, 119 people), withdrawal that began and ended earlier (all 8 trials that described the time course), shorter time in treatment (standardized difference -1.07, -1.31 to -0.83; 3 trials, 310 people), and about twice as many people with low blood pressure or other side effects (151 against 79 in 1,000; risk ratio 1.92, 1.19 to 3.10; 6 trials, 464 people), an excess that was no longer statistically clear without the three trials at high risk of bias (2.02, 0.62 to 6.64). Completion did not differ clearly (risk ratio 0.85, 0.69 to 1.05; 9 trials, 659 people), but the interval still allows a meaningful advantage for methadone. In three small direct comparisons that could not be pooled, lofexidine lowered blood pressure less than clonidine. Neither approach fully relieved aches, poor sleep, low energy, chills or anxiety. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Compared with a slowly reducing course of methadone, clonidine-type medicines gave about the same overall withdrawal, but it came and went sooner, treatment was shorter, and side effects such as low blood pressure and dizziness were about twice as common. About as many people finished either way. Lofexidine lowered blood pressure less than clonidine in a few small studies. Neither approach took away all the aches, bad sleep and anxiety.
population: People dependent on opioids (heroin or methadone) in supervised withdrawal, mostly inpatient, in 12 randomized trials pooled in a Cochrane review
exposure: Clonidine, lofexidine or guanfacine as the main withdrawal medicine
outcome: Withdrawal severity and time course, time in treatment, adverse effects and completion of withdrawal treatment
magnitude: Overall severity SMD 0.13 (-0.24 to 0.49), 3 trials, 119, moderate; peak severity SMD 0.22 (-0.02 to 0.46), 2 trials, 263, moderate; severe withdrawal RR 1.18 (0.81 to 1.73), 5 trials, 340, low. Time in treatment SMD -1.07 (-1.31 to -0.83), 3 trials, 310, low. Hypotensive or other adverse effects RR 1.92 (1.19 to 3.10), 6 trials, 464, low (79 against 151 per 1000); without three high-risk trials RR 2.02 (0.62 to 6.64), 203; drop-out for adverse effects RR 3.62 (0.77 to 16.94), 4 trials, 153, no events with methadone. Completion RR 0.85 (0.69 to 1.05), 9 trials, 659, low (568 against 483 per 1000); heroin RR 0.87 (0.61 to 1.25), methadone RR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18); inpatient RR 0.87 (0.68 to 1.12), outpatient RR 1.09 (0.73 to 1.64).

evidence.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › 2 › (a) Withdrawal syndrome › Intensity of withdrawal, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Against reducing doses of methadone: severe withdrawal RR 1.18 (0.81 to 1.73), 5 trials, 340 participants, GRADE low; peak withdrawal score SMD 0.22 (-0.02 to 0.46), 2 trials, 263, moderate; overall severity SMD 0.13 (-0.24 to 0.49), 3 trials, 119, moderate.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 2 › (a) Time course of withdrawal, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: In all eight trials that described the time course, withdrawal signs and symptoms appeared earlier and resolved sooner with an alpha2 agonist; with tapered methadone, withdrawal in general peaked late, at the end of the taper.

evidence.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › 2 › (b) Duration of treatment, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Time in treatment shorter with an alpha2 agonist than with reducing doses of methadone: SMD -1.07 (-1.31 to -0.83), 3 trials, 310 participants, GRADE low; SMD -1.04 (-1.44 to -0.64) without the high-risk trial.

evidence.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › 2 › (c) Nature and incidence of adverse effects, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Hypotensive or other adverse effects, alpha2 agonist against reducing doses of methadone: RR 1.92 (1.19 to 3.10), 6 trials, 464 participants, GRADE low; illustrative 79 per 1000 with methadone against 151 per 1000 with an alpha2 agonist; without the three high-risk trials RR 2.02 (0.62 to 6.64), 203 participants. Drop-out for adverse effects RR 3.62 (0.77 to 16.94), 4 trials, 153 participants, no events in methadone arms. In one trial 89 of 100 people on clonidine had dizziness on standing.

evidence.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › 2 › (d) Completion of treatment, 4th paragraph; Effect of opioid used; Effect of treatment setting
evidence.extracted: Completion, alpha2 agonist against reducing doses of methadone: RR 0.85 (0.69 to 1.05), 9 trials, 659 participants, GRADE low (selection bias, heterogeneity); illustrative 568 per 1000 with methadone against 483 per 1000 with an alpha2 agonist; without San 1990 RR 0.91 (0.75 to 1.11). People withdrawing from heroin RR 0.87 (0.61 to 1.25); from methadone RR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18); inpatient RR 0.87 (0.68 to 1.12), I2 67%; outpatient RR 1.09 (0.73 to 1.64).

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 3. Clonidine compared to lofexidine or guanfacine › (d) Nature and incidence of adverse effects › Hypotension, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Postural hypotension in 8 of 14 on lofexidine against 13 of 14 on clonidine (Kahn 1997); doses withheld for low blood pressure on 4.1% of occasions with lofexidine against 8.9% with clonidine (Lin 1997); not pooled.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Summary of main results › 2. (a) Withdrawal syndrome experienced, 2nd paragraph; Potential biases in the review process, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Neither alpha2 agonists nor a methadone taper appeared to fully suppress aches and pains, sleep disturbance, loss of energy, chills or anxiety. The authors note that fixed methadone tapers in the trials, unlike flexible tapers in practice, would be expected to bias the comparison against methadone.

risk_of_bias.note: Several trials at high or unclear risk of selection or attrition bias; the adverse-effect excess loses significance without them; fixed trial tapers bias against methadone.

inconsistency.note: Completion shows heterogeneity (inpatient I2 67%), but the claim states no clear difference; the time-course finding was the same in all eight trials.

indirectness.note: Worded for supervised withdrawal from heroin or methadone in these trials.

imprecision.note: Small numbers for severity and duration; few adverse-effect events; the completion interval includes both no difference and a meaningful advantage for methadone.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review; recorded as unknown.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give low, in line with the review's own ratings (low for severe withdrawal, duration, adverse effects and completion; moderate for the two severity scores). Worded as an association because the certainty is low. Status replicated: up to nine trials per outcome from several countries; the time-course pattern was consistent across eight trials.
